title: Aussie driver stung with $1,300 fine over little known phone law
text:
By ASHLEY NICKEL, NEWS REPORTER, AUSTRALIA

Published:  18:17 AEST, 21 September 2026   |  Updated:  01:44 AEST, 22 September 2026

80

View  comments

An Australian motorist has lashed out at road fines being too steep after she was hit with almost $1,300 in penalties for wearing a phone on a lanyard.

The Queenslander, from the Sunshine Coast, was fined $1,295 and lost four demerit points earlier this month when she was caught on one of the state's AI-cameras.

She told Yahoo News on Monday that she hadn't known it was illegal to wear her phone on a lanyard while driving.

The fine noted the phone was 'resting on' her body, an infringement caught by Queensland's AI-powered road monitoring cameras.

The driver thought it would be fine to wear the device as she wasn't touching or using it.

However, she was too scared to take the matter to court due to the possibility of hefty court fees on top of the already steep fine.

'I sent an explanation letter, but it was dismissed. It's ludicrous to be hit with a $1,295 fine and four demerit points,' she said.

The same $1,295 fine and loss of four demerit points applies to drivers caught using their phone or incorrectly wearing their seatbelt.

A Queensland driver was fined $1,295 for wearing her phone on a lanyard (above) while driving

The Queenslander considered taking the fine (above) to court as she was unaware of the law but was worried about facing further expenses

The woman (above) said it was 'ludicrous' to be hit with such a fine for not handling the phone

That fine rose by 3.5 per cent from July 1 under the state's annual indexation policy.

Repeat offenders caught committing the same crime within a year can also face double demerit point loss.

RACQ's Head of Public Policy, Dr Michael Kane, questioned whether steep fines were an effective deterrent for dangerous drivers.

He highlighted the continued rise in road deaths despite the increase of penalties.

'Dangerous drivers must be held to account, but RACQ also supports a comprehensive review of traffic fines and penalties to improve consistency, change behaviour and make Queensland roads safer, including considering incentives for road users who do the right thing,' Dr Kane said.

He instead pushed for Queensland to 'get serious on road safety through a penalty system that genuinely improves culture'.

Queensland recorded 214 road deaths between the beginning of January and the end of August 2026.

Are fines this steep for minor phone offences fair or just punishing everyday drivers too harshly?
